_description: Legal/regulatory real-doc corpus: two cross-referencing US statutes (FOIA 5 U.S.C. 552 + Privacy Act 5 U.S.C. 552a). Stresses the CROSS-REFERENCE + DEFINED-TERM failure mode — grounding a claim that depends on a specific numbered exemption/subsection/condition or a precise statutory definition, where general world knowledge of FOIA/Privacy-Act is insufficient (memorization-resistant). Public-domain US-gov PDFs (govinfo.gov); sources LOCAL in ~/corpus-drop/legal, not committed.
_labelling_rule: _anchor_phrase = verbatim distinctive substring of the answer chunk; resolve fills relevant_chunk_ids. answer_must_mention = list-of-lists of required answer elements (synonyms within each inner list). Counterfactuals carry _counterfactual_mode.
_source_note: FOIA=foia-5usc552.pdf (5 U.S.C. 552), PrivacyAct=privacy-act-5usc552a.pdf (5 U.S.C. 552a); both govinfo USCODE-2023-title5.
_authoring: generate(2 deep-readers)->adversarial-verify(per-candidate) workflow + deterministic resolve + full-eval gate.

queries.question: Under FOIA's definitions, what does the term "search" mean for purposes of paragraph (a)(3) when an agency responds to a records request?
queries._anchor_phrase: means to review, manually or by automated means, agency records for the purpose of locating
queries._expected_answer: "Search" means to review, manually or by automated means, agency records for the purpose of locating those records which are responsive to a request.
queries._grounding_quote: (D) For purposes of this paragraph, the term ‘‘search’’ means to review, manually or by automated means, agency records for the purpose of locating those records which are responsive to a request.
queries._memorization_resistance: The statute supplies a precise, narrow defined-term boundary at (a)(3)(D): "search" = review (manually or by automated means) for the purpose of LOCATING responsive records. A model relying on the ordinary meaning of "search" would not reproduce this exact statutory scope, which counterintuitively equates search with "review" even though search and review are separate fee categories elsewhere in the statute.

queries.question: In FOIA's expedited-processing provisions, how does the statute define a "compelling need"?
queries._anchor_phrase: could reasonably be expected to pose an imminent threat to the life or physical safety of an individual
queries._expected_answer: A compelling need means (I) that a failure to obtain the records on an expedited basis could reasonably be expected to pose an imminent threat to the life or physical safety of an individual; or (II) with respect to a person primarily engaged in disseminating information, urgency to inform the public concerning actual or alleged Federal Government activity.
queries._grounding_quote: (v) For purposes of this subparagraph, the term ‘‘compelling need’’ means— (I) that a failure to obtain requested records on an expedited basis under this paragraph could reasonably be expected to pose an imminent threat to the life or physical safety of an individual; or (II) with respect to a request made by a person primarily engaged in disseminating information, urgency to inform the public concerning actual or alleged Federal Government activity.
queries._memorization_resistance: Requires the exact two-pronged statutory definition at (a)(6)(E)(v) (imminent threat to life/safety + urgency to inform the public concerning actual or alleged Federal Government activity), not a general notion of urgency; answer_must_mention enforces both prongs.

queries._grounding_quote: (ii) For purposes of this subparagraph, the term ‘‘exceptional circumstances’’ does not include a delay that results from a predictable agency workload of requests under this section, unless the agency demonstrates reasonable progress in reducing its backlog of pending requests.
queries._memorization_resistance: The exclusion (predictable workload does NOT count, with the backlog-progress carve-out) is a specific negative-scope rule in (a)(6)(C)(ii) that general FOIA knowledge would not supply verbatim.

queries.question: What is the statute of limitations — the deadline after a final agency denial — for filing a FOIA lawsuit in federal district court under 5 U.S.C. § 552?
queries._expected_answer: REFUSE — 5 U.S.C. § 552 (FOIA) states no limitations period (deadline) for filing a FOIA lawsuit. The text only sets a 20-day agency determination clock (a)(6)(A)(i), a 30-day deadline for the defendant to answer a complaint (a)(4)(C), and a 'not less than 90 days' administrative appeal window (a)(6)(A)(i)(III)(aa) — none of which is a statute of limitations to bring suit. Note: the 'within two years' period in the Privacy Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552a(g)(5), is a DIFFERENT statute and a different cause of action; it does not supply a FOIA suit-filing deadline. The text does not answer this question.
queries._grounding_quote: Confirmed ABSENT from both statutes: no provision of 5 U.S.C. § 552 states a limitations period for filing a FOIA lawsuit (grep for 'limitation'/'years from'/'brought within'/'cause of action' returns no suit-filing deadline; the only 'X years from the date' hit is an unrelated Executive Order Working Group termination). The near-miss texts are verbatim present — 'the defendant shall serve an answer or otherwise plead to any complaint made under this subsection within thirty days after service' (a)(4)(C); 'determine within 20 days' (a)(6)(A)(i); 'within a period determined by the head of the agency that is not less than 90 days after the date of such adverse determination' (a)(6)(A)(i)(III)(aa) — but none is a statute of limitations to bring suit. The Privacy Act's 'within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises' (§ 552a(g)(5)) is a different statute and cause of action, not a FOIA suit-filing deadline.
queries._memorization_resistance: The question is phrased to pull the FOIA 30-day defendant-answer clock (a)(4)(C), the 20-day determination clock, or the not-less-than-90-day appeal window as if one were the suit-filing deadline, and — across the combined corpus — to pull the Privacy Act's 'within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises' (§ 552a(g)(5)) as a false FOIA answer. Correct refusal requires recognizing from the text that none of the FOIA timing provisions is a limitations period and that the PA two-year window belongs to a separate statute/cause of action; § 552's actual SOL (28 U.S.C. § 2401(a)) is in neither document.

queries.question: Under 5 U.S.C. § 552, what is the maximum per-page dollar amount an agency may charge for duplicating records?
queries._expected_answer: REFUSE — § 552 sets no per-page dollar duplication charge. It limits fees to "reasonable standard charges" for duplication and waives fees for the first one hundred pages of duplication (for certain non-commercial/news-media requesters), but states no fixed per-page rate; the only dollar figure in the statute is the $250 advance-payment threshold.
queries._grounding_quote: The fee provisions limit charges to “reasonable standard charges for document ... duplication” (a)(4)(A)(ii) and waive fees for “the first one hundred pages of duplication” (a)(4)(A)(iv)(II); the only dollar figure in the statute is the $250 advance-payment threshold in (a)(4)(A)(v) — no per-page dollar amount is stated anywhere.
queries._memorization_resistance: Retrieval surfaces the fee/duplication and 100-free-pages provisions, tempting a model to fabricate a specific per-page rate (e.g. the common $0.10/page found in agency FOIA fee SCHEDULES, which is not in the statute itself); the statute only says "reasonable standard charges," so the correct response is refusal.

queries.question: According to 5 U.S.C. § 552, what is the maximum prison sentence an agency official can receive for willfully and unlawfully withholding records from a requester?
queries._expected_answer: REFUSE — § 552 (FOIA) specifies NO criminal penalty or prison sentence for withholding records; its enforcement is civil (court-ordered production, attorney fees, contempt, and a Special Counsel disciplinary referral). The only criminal penalties in this title appear in the Privacy Act, § 552a(i), and even those are misdemeanors 'fined not more than $5,000' for wrongful DISCLOSURE — not withholding — with no term of imprisonment specified anywhere. No maximum prison sentence exists to state.
queries._grounding_quote: FOIA § 552 enforcement is civil — injunctive production (a)(4)(B), attorney fees (a)(4)(E), a Special Counsel disciplinary referral (a)(4)(F), and 'the district court may punish for contempt the responsible employee' (a)(4)(G); no criminal prison term appears in § 552. The only 'CRIMINAL PENALTIES' in the title are in § 552a(i), which make the named conduct 'a misdemeanor and fined not more than $5,000' — a fine, not imprisonment, and for disclosure rather than withholding.
queries._memorization_resistance: FOIA contains no criminal-penalty provision at all, so any specific prison-term answer is fabricated. The trap is real: § 552a(i) is explicitly headed 'CRIMINAL PENALTIES' and keys on 'willfully' and 'officer or employee of an agency', so a model may latch onto it and invent a sentence — yet the actual text imposes only a '$5,000' fine (no imprisonment) and is for wrongful disclosure, not withholding. Distinguishing this requires the statutory text, not general FOIA knowledge.

queries.question: What is the limitations period for bringing a civil action to enforce a liability created under the Privacy Act?
queries._anchor_phrase: within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises
queries._expected_answer: The action may be brought within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises (with a special rule extending it to two years after the individual discovers a material and willful misrepresentation).
queries._grounding_quote: An action to enforce any liability created under this section may be brought in the district court of the United States in the district in which the complainant resides, or has his principal place of business, or in which the agency records are situated, or in the District of Columbia, without regard to the amount in controversy, within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises, except that where an agency has materially and willfully misrepresented any information required under this section to be disclosed to an individual and the information so misrepresented is material to establishment of the liability of the agency to the individual under this section, the action may be brought at any time within two years after discovery by the individual of the misrepresentation.
queries._memorization_resistance: A precise statute-of-limitations figure (two years) under Privacy Act subsection (g)(5). It is distinct from FOIA's administrative deadlines (FOIA contains no such provision), and the exact period plus the two-years-after-discovery extension for material/willful misrepresentation is memorization-resistant.
